spec.title: Routing: the table, the match, the plan and the receipt

item.title: The plan: from a row to jobs
The receipt and the failure note
Rows and codes this domain owns

spec.purpose: Routing applies the routes table to one record and returns a plan: the row that matched and the jobs it implies, in order. It is a pure function of the record, the table and the escalation count; it performs nothing.

section.title: What routing decides

node.title: Routing is a pure function of the record, the routes table and the escalation count: the first matching row decides, the plan it returns is data, and no Go branch reads a kind, a code or a note outside a row match

section.text: In: a Record with its claim, the loaded Table, the escalation count for its ticket. Out: a Plan. The engine turns the plan's job specs into stored jobs; routing never touches the store or the executor.

section.title: Loading the table
section.text: The table is the routes file named in the configuration, decoded with unknown keys refused: schema version, description, max attempts 3, and rows with match, do, and the parameters the schema allows.

Checks at load: do is one of enqueue, wake, seat, escalate, notify_owner, break-glass, ignore, none; every row but ignore names to; down is tester, reviewer or merger; with is ticket, pr, record or verify; line is done or decision.
A table that fails at start is exit 3 naming the row index and the key; a table that fails on reload is kept out, the loaded one stays, and one 500 note names the file.
Table.Version is the content hash of the loaded file; the status answer and every plan carry it, so a parity mismatch can say which table decided.

section.title: The match: first row wins
section.text: A row matches when every key its match names holds: kind equal, code equal, code at or above code_gte, attempt equal, attempt below attempt_lt, escalations equal, escalations below escalations_lt. An absent key holds for every record.
Rows are tried top to bottom and the first that holds decides; the order of the file is the behaviour, which is why the table is data and the loader keeps the order.
A record with no attempt matches as attempt 1.

The escalation count is the number of escalated records on the same ticket, written by a runner seat, whose id sorts before this record. Runner seats are the configured list, so counts survive the cut-over.
Match takes values and returns a row or none; the escalation count is computed by the engine from intake's records and passed in, so the function needs no file system.

section.title: The plan: from a row to jobs
section.text: A plan lists, in order: the primary job the row's do implies, the down job when the row names down, and the receipt job. Each later job names the earlier ones in After, so the job runner keeps the order.

The down runs even when the primary is dead-lettered: the gate record is on disk either way, the seat is finished, and a failed action is never retried past its attempts; the down's After allows dead as well as done.
The receipt is a record job that runs after the primary and the down, and only when the primary is done; a dead primary gets the failure note of the jobs domain instead, and the ledger says failed.

Seat names come from the role file's label with the ticket substituted and lowercased, through the seats domain; a role whose label still holds a variable after substitution is a plan failure naming the role.
The wake line is: record, the id, then pr and sha when the row says with pr and the record carries them, then playbook and the playbook path for the row's to. Nothing else reaches a seat's prompt.
A pr that is not a positive integer or a sha that is not 7 to 40 lowercase hex is a plan failure naming the record; neither is passed on, because both reach a prompt as typed text.
seat, enqueue and down need a ticket; a row that asks for one on a record without one is a plan failure naming the action.

section.title: Actions, one by one
section.text: wake: one prompt job to the seat the row's to names for the record's ticket, with the wake line.

seat: a seat-up job for the ticket and the row's role, then the same prompt job after it. The seat script leaves a live seat as it is, so the job runs for every record and never asks whether the seat is up.
notify_owner: one prompt job to the interface seat with record, the id, line, the row's line, playbook and the interface playbook path.
enqueue: one enqueue job with the ticket, the record id as from, and the record's priority when it is p0 to p3.
escalate: one record job that writes an escalated record with the row's code, addressed to the row's to, on the ticket, whose note names the escalated record id.
break-glass: one break-glass job for the record's seat with the record id; the seat script reads the owner's answer itself and refuses with exit 3, which is a handled result, never a failure.
none: no primary job; the receipt still records that the record was seen.
ignore: no job at all; the ledger word is the only trace, so a seat coming up does not cost a receipt.
down: one seat-down job for the role's seat on the ticket; the seat script's second down prints already down and exits 0, so two gate records for one ticket cost nothing.

section.title: The receipt and the failure note
section.text: The receipt is record.routed 300, addressed to the row's to, on the record's ticket when it has one, with the routed file's repo-relative path as evidence.
Its note: routed, kind, code, the id in parentheses, colon, the action and the to, then comma down and the role when the row had one.
The board reads receipts to place a ticket at a station; the shape is kept byte for byte so the board needs no change on cut-over.
The failure note is a 500 note to the monitor on the ticket: route failed for, kind, code, record, the id, colon, the reason the executor or the plan gave, cut to the writer's limit.
The failure note is written by the jobs domain when the primary is dead-lettered, once, with the last reason; the ledger word becomes failed at the same moment.

section.title: No row, ignore, own
section.text: A record no row matches is ledgered unrouted and one 500 note to the monitor says no route for, kind, code, record, the id. Routing does not guess.
The replay fixtures carry one case per row, so a row nobody exercises fails the suite; a kind the schema allows with no row at all is reported by the check subcommand as a gap, not at runtime.
Own records never reach routing; intake ledgers them first.

section.title: Keys this domain reads
section.key: Where role files are read for seat labels.
Where the wake line's playbook path points; the path is written as the seat will read it, on the host.
Seats whose escalated records count toward escalations.

section.title: Rows and codes this domain owns
section.owns-route: enqueue to the architect's queue, priority from the request.
wake the worker with the ticket.
seat the tester with the pr.
seat the reviewer with the pr, down the tester.
seat the merger with the pr, down the reviewer.
wake the architect to verify, down the merger.
wake the worker with the record, down the merger.
notify the owner through the interface agent, line done.
ignore: a receipt is never routed.
section.owns-code: The thing happened: a merge landed, a default was applied, a break glass was granted.
A gate passed: test, review, verify.
The receipt: the scheduler saw the record and performed its row; also a request forwarded into the line.
The merge could not land; the worker merges main.

section.case: A first 423 and a second 423 are told apart.

example.text: pr.opened 100 on a ticket: the plan is seat-up tester, prompt record id playbook tester, receipt record.routed 300 to tester.
test.failed 422 attempt 3: the plan is an escalated 423 record to the architect, then down the tester, then the receipt.
Routing reads the note field and decides the worker probably needs more context.
example.why: Routing is the table; a note is for humans.
